Produced chemically by reduction of potassium nitrate.
A nitrite salt. In sucuk, salami, sausages and ham it preserves the pink colour and prevents the growth of the botulism bacterium.

IARC classifies the ingestion of nitrite and nitrate under conditions that may lead to the formation of nitrosamines in the body as Group 2A (probably carcinogenic). It is used in processed meats such as sucuk, sausages and salami to preserve colour and prevent botulism.
Produced chemically by absorbing nitrogen oxide gases from nitric acid production into a sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate solution.
A nitrate salt; it is converted to nitrite in the body and in meat. Used in cured meats and some cheeses.

IARC classifies the ingestion of nitrite and nitrate under conditions that may lead to the formation of nitrosamines in the body as Group 2A (probably carcinogenic). It is used in processed meats such as sucuk, sausages and salami to preserve colour and prevent botulism.
Mostly obtained from natural deposits (caliche) in Chile by dissolving them in brine and crystallising; it may also be produced chemically.
A nitrate salt (saltpetre). Used in cured meats and some cheeses.

Produced by fermentation of carbohydrates or by chemical synthesis (from acetaldehyde, butane or methanol).

The potassium salt of acetic acid (vinegar acid); acetate is part of the body's normal metabolism. In 1973 JECFA set the group ADI for acetic acid and its potassium/sodium salts as 'not limited'; the decision was maintained in 1997.
Acetic acid may be produced by fermentation or by chemical synthesis; its salts are obtained by neutralising the acid.
The sodium salts of acetic acid. They regulate acidity, give a vinegar taste to crisp seasonings and prevent mould in bakery products.

The sodium salt of acetic acid (vinegar acid); acetate is part of the body's normal metabolism. In 1973 JECFA set the group ADI for acetic acid and its potassium/sodium salts as 'not limited'; the decision was maintained in 1997. In addition, an ADI of 0–15 mg/kg body weight/day was set for sodium diacetate.
Obtained by neutralising acetic acid with sodium carbonate; acetic acid may be produced by fermentation or by chemical synthesis.
The calcium salt of acetic acid. Used as an acidity regulator, preservative and firming agent.
The calcium salt of acetic acid (vinegar acid); acetate is part of the body's normal metabolism. In 1973 JECFA set the ADI as 'not limited'.
Obtained by neutralising acetic acid with calcium hydroxide; acetic acid may be produced by fermentation or by chemical synthesis.
The acid formed by fermentation that gives yoghurt and pickles their sourness. Today it is usually produced by fermentation of sugar or starch; used as an acidity regulator.
Produced by lactic fermentation of sugars or by chemical synthesis.
An organic acid that also forms naturally in cheese. It prevents mould in bread and bakery products.
Mostly produced by chemical synthesis from petrochemical raw materials; its salts are obtained by neutralising the acid.
The sodium salt of propionic acid. It prevents mould in bread and bakery products.
Mostly produced by chemical synthesis from petrochemical raw materials; its salts are obtained by neutralising the acid.
The calcium salt of propionic acid. It is the most widely used mould inhibitor in packaged bread.
Mostly produced by chemical synthesis from petrochemical raw materials; its salts are obtained by neutralising the acid.
The potassium salt of propionic acid. Used as a mould inhibitor in bakery products.
Mostly produced by chemical synthesis from petrochemical raw materials; its salts are obtained by neutralising the acid.
A boron-containing acid. In the EU it is permitted in food only in sturgeon caviar.
In the EU it is permitted only for caviar (sturgeon roe); boric acid falls under reproductive toxicity (Category 1B) in the EU classification.
Obtained by treating boron minerals such as borax, kernite or colemanite with sulphuric or hydrochloric acid.
A boron-containing mineral salt (borax). In the EU it is permitted in food only in sturgeon caviar.

In the EU it is permitted only for caviar (sturgeon roe). Borax (disodium tetraborate) is classified as reproductive toxicity Category 1B in the EU CLP classification (H360FD; Regulation 790/2009). In 2013 EFSA set a group ADI for boric acid and borax of 0.16 mg/kg body weight/day, expressed as boron.
Obtained by grinding sodium borate ore, dissolving it in hot water and crystallising it (physical processing).
Carbon dioxide gas. It gives fizz to carbonated drinks, replaces air in packaging and plays a role in leavening.
Collected as a by-product of fermentation, from natural sources or from industrial processes.
An acid found naturally in fruits such as apples. It gives a sour taste and is used in confectionery, drinks and jams.
DL-malic acid is produced by chemical synthesis from petrochemical raw material; its salts are obtained by neutralisation.
An organic acid that also occurs in nature. It gives a sour taste and is used in powdered drinks, jellies and desserts.
Produced by chemical synthesis; it is a molecule that also occurs in nature.
Vitamin C. As an antioxidant it prevents discolouration in fruit juices and meat products, and it is a flour treatment agent in bread.
Produced from glucose by fermentation and chemical steps; it is the same molecule as the vitamin C found in nature.
The sodium salt of vitamin C. It helps preserve colour in meat products and is used as an antioxidant.
Obtained by neutralising vitamin C (ascorbic acid) with sodium bicarbonate; ascorbic acid is produced from glucose by fermentation and chemical steps.
The calcium salt of vitamin C. It is used as an antioxidant and as a source of vitamin C.
Obtained by reacting vitamin C (ascorbic acid) with calcium carbonate; ascorbic acid is produced from glucose by fermentation and chemical steps.
The fat-soluble form of vitamin C (ascorbyl palmitate, etc.). It delays fats from going rancid.
Obtained by esterification of ascorbic acid with palmitic acid (chemically or enzymatically).
An antioxidant from the vitamin E family. It is obtained from vegetable oils or synthesised, and it delays the spoilage of fats.
Obtained by vacuum steam distillation of vegetable oils.
An antioxidant from the vitamin E family. It is obtained from vegetable oils or synthesised, and it delays the spoilage of fats.
A tocopherol (a form of vitamin E) produced by chemical synthesis.
An antioxidant from the vitamin E family. It is obtained from vegetable oils or synthesised, and it delays the spoilage of fats.

Produced by chemical reaction of gallic acid with alcohols.
A synthetic antioxidant obtained from gallic acid. It delays fats from going rancid and is used in fats, oils and fatty products.
No longer permitted as a food additive in the EU: it was removed from the permitted list by Regulation (EU) 2018/1481 (in 2015 EFSA found no data with which to assess its safety).
Not permitted in Türkiye: it is not on the list of permitted additives in the Turkish Food Codex Regulation on Food Additives (2023) (Ministry guidance, October 2024).
Produced by chemical reaction of gallic acid with alcohols.

Produced by chemical reaction of gallic acid with alcohols.
An antioxidant structurally similar to vitamin C. It preserves colour in processed meats and speeds up nitrite curing.
Produced by fermentation of glucose by bacteria (Pseudomonas) to 2-keto-D-gluconic acid, followed by chemical steps.
The sodium salt of erythorbic acid. It preserves colour in processed meats.
Produced from glucose in steps combining fermentation and chemical synthesis (via 2-keto-D-gluconic acid).
A petroleum-derived synthetic antioxidant. It delays rancidity in frying oils and fatty snacks.
Produced chemically by reacting hydroquinone with isobutylene or tert-butyl alcohol.
A petroleum-derived synthetic antioxidant. It delays rancidity in fats, chewing gum and cereal products.

Group 2B according to IARC (possibly carcinogenic). In 2011 EFSA set the acceptable daily intake at 1 mg/kg. In the EU its use is subject to maximum levels; it may be found in frying oils, powdered soups and seasonings.
Produced chemically by reacting 4-hydroxyanisole with isobutylene (or from hydroquinone).
A petroleum-derived synthetic antioxidant. It delays rancidity in fats, chewing gum and packaging.
Produced by chemical synthesis by reacting p-cresol with isobutylene; its raw materials are obtained from petroleum and coal tar.
A natural emulsifier obtained from soya, sunflower, rapeseed or egg. It allows fat and water to mix in chocolate, margarine and bakery products.
Mostly obtained from soya or sunflower; relevant for people with soya allergy. In the EU, GM soya must be labelled; products from outside the EU may be derived from GM soya.
Obtained by physical methods from foods such as soya, sunflower or egg.
The sodium salt of lactic acid. It retains moisture in meat products, extends shelf life and regulates acidity.
Obtained by neutralising lactic acid; lactic acid may be produced by fermentation or by chemical synthesis.
The potassium salt of lactic acid. It is used as an acidity regulator and humectant.
Obtained by neutralising lactic acid; lactic acid may be produced by fermentation or by chemical synthesis.

Obtained by neutralising lactic acid; lactic acid may be produced by fermentation or by chemical synthesis.

Mostly produced by fermentation of sugars with the mould Aspergillus niger (sometimes with Candida yeast).
Sodium salts of citric acid. They regulate acidity and are used as emulsifying salts in processed cheese and to soften sourness in drinks.
Obtained by neutralising citric acid with sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate.
Potassium salts of citric acid. They are used as acidity regulators in drinks and desserts.

Calcium salts of citric acid. They are an acidity regulator, a firming agent and a source of calcium.

Obtained by neutralising the tartar in wine lees with sodium hydroxide or sodium carbonate and purifying it.

A natural antioxidant obtained from rosemary leaves. It delays rancidity in fats, meat products and sauces.

Obtained by partial hydrolysis of animal collagen.

A weighting agent produced from sugar. It prevents flavouring oils from rising to the surface in cloudy fruit drinks.

Obtained chemically by neutralising phosphoric acid produced from phosphate rock with sodium or potassium hydroxide and drying it above 250 °C.
Polyphosphates: phosphate salts. They retain water in processed meat, seafood and processed cheese.

A ring-shaped sugar molecule produced from starch using enzymes. It holds flavourings and vitamins and stabilises them.

Cellulose, the main building block of plant fibres. In powder form it prevents caking and is a bulking agent in products such as grated cheese.

In the EU, the label warning ("releases formaldehyde") depends not on a single preservative but on the total formaldehyde that may be released in the product: if the total exceeds 0.001%, the warning is mandatory. More than one releaser increases this total.
Caution in combination: more than one phosphate additive
Phosphate

In 2019 EFSA set a group daily intake limit for phosphate additives, expressed as phosphorus (40 mg/kg body weight), and reported that this limit may be exceeded in infants, children and adolescents who consume a lot of foods containing phosphates. The limit applies to the total of all phosphate additives.
Caution in combination: more than one synthetic antioxidant
Propyl gallate, TBHQ, BHA
Under the EU additives regulation, if propyl gallate, TBHQ and BHA are used together, the amount of each must be reduced proportionally; the maximum level applies to the total.
Caution in combination: more than one glutamate
Glutamate

In 2017 EFSA set a group daily intake limit for all six of glutamic acid and its salts (E 620–625): 30 mg/kg body weight. It reported that some groups, especially young children, may exceed this limit. The limit applies to the total of all glutamate additives.
Caution in combination: more than one sulphite
Sulphite

In cosmetics, the EU limit for inorganic sulphites and bisulphites is calculated as free sulphur dioxide; all sulphites in the same product count together towards this limit. This is also important for people with sulphite sensitivity.
Caution in combination: more than one quaternary ammonium conditioning agent
Cetrimonium / steartrimonium / behentrimonium chloride

In products such as hair conditioners, the EU limit for these substances is set not individually but on their total when used together (a total of 2.5% in rinse-off hair products, or 5% with behentrimonium).
Caution in combination: nitrite + nitrate
Nitrite
Nitrate

Nitrate is partly converted to nitrite in the body. In 2017 EFSA reported that intake from additives alone remained within safe limits, but that when all sources, such as vegetables and water, are counted together the limit may be exceeded in every age group. It assessed the contribution of nitrite used at authorised levels to nitrosamine formation as being of low concern.

Substance that must not be used with nitrosating substances
Substance that may form nitrosamines

Some amines may form nitrosamines together with substances such as nitrite or bronopol; some nitrosamines are carcinogenic. For this reason, the EU Cosmetics Regulation requires that these amines are "not to be used with nitrosating systems". Both groups appear together in this product.
Caution in combination: more than one paraben
Paraben
In the EU, parabens have a total limit in addition to their individual limits: the total of propyl and butyl paraben may not exceed 0.14%, and the total of all parabens may not exceed 0.8%.

Hydrogen peroxide or a substance releasing it

Polyol

The laxative effect of polyols depends on the total amount. Under EU rules, if the total of added polyols exceeds 10%, the label must carry the warning "excessive consumption may produce laxative effects".
Caution in combination: more than one polysorbate
Polysorbate
In 2015 EFSA set a group daily intake limit for polysorbates (E 432–436): 25 mg/kg body weight. The limit applies to the total of all polysorbates.

Salicylic acid / salicylate
The EU limit for salicylic acid and its salts is calculated as the acid and assessed together. They are not used in products intended for children under 3 years of age (except shampoos).

Sorbic acid / sorbate
The EU limit for sorbic acid and its salts as preservatives is 0.6%, calculated as the acid; those present in the same product count together towards this limit.

Sodium benzoate

In the 2007 Southampton study, children were given these colours together with sodium benzoate as a mixture, and a possible effect on behaviour was observed. This product contains the same pair. Sulphite
The threshold for the sulphite allergen applies to the total, not to individual substances: if total sulphur dioxide exceeds 10 mg/kg (or 10 mg/L), it must be declared on the label as an allergen.

Thioglycolate
The EU limit for thioglycolates used in perms, hair straighteners and depilatories is calculated as thioglycolic acid; all thioglycolates in the same product count together towards this limit.

Liquid laundry detergent capsules are subject to special rules in the EU (CLP Annex II 3.3): the outer packaging must be opaque, have a lockable closure that is difficult for children to open, and carry the statement "Keep out of reach of children" (P102). The capsule film must contain a bitter substance that causes a child to spit it out within 6 seconds of putting it in the mouth, and the film must withstand water for 30 seconds and a pressure of 300 N. These rules were introduced because of swallowing and eye-contact accidents involving young children who mistake capsules for sweets.
